newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea firms' second-half earnings seen improving.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea firms' second-half earnings seen improving.

text.p: A sluggish domestic economy, weak global memory chip prices and high oil costs contributed to a lacklustre first-half performance by key South Korean companies, but analysts said on Friday they expected better full-year results.
Auto and semiconductor manufacturers took a hit, as did the country's electricity monopoly, Korea Electric Power Corp. But half-year results for steel giant Pohang Iron and Steel Co sparkled.

"For major companies, my gut feeling is that earnings were probably worse than expected," said Lee Keunmo, head of research at ING Barings Securities. "As far as the full year is concerned, I think there definitely will be an improvement."
Del Ricks, head of research at BZW Securities, said profits would improve as companies emerged from a cyclical downturn.
"Last year was a bad year, but really it was the second half of 1996 that was bad. I think most securities houses are looking for fairly strong full-year earnings growth," Ricks said.
Daishin Economic Research Institute found first-half net profits of affiliates of the top 30 business groups were off 26 percent from a year earlier, while sales were down 15 percent.
Weak global memory prices hammered chip manufacturers.
Prices of 16-megabit dynamic random access memory chips or DRAMs, the mainstay of computer memory chips, have been in the $6-$10 range this year, down from $18-$48 a year earlier.
First-half net profits at Samsung Electronics, the world's largest DRAM maker, tumbled 73 percent to 123.2 billion won ($137.8 million) from 453.4 billion a year ago.
Samsung's interim results were lifted by information technology sales of 2.05 trillion won, up from 1.05 trillion.
LG Semicon saw its first-half net plunge 88 percent to 16 billion won from 131.4 billion a year ago.

"LG Semicon has no support from other divisions. It reflects the real story in DRAMs. Now we're seeing the bottom of the cycle for DRAM prices. I'm positive about semiconductor companies' prospects in the second half," Lee said.
South Korean car makers saw first-half exports expand, but not enough to offset slowing domestic sales and the lingering effects from January's nationwide labour strikes.
Heated competition at home which resulted in no-interest loans and deep cash discounts exacerbated automakers' troubles.

To no one's surprise, Kia Motors Corp's first-half losses widened to 37.0 billion won from 10.34 billion a year ago. Its parent Kia Group was put under protection of creditor banks until September 29.
But analysts said weaker interim results reported by top-ranked Hyundai Motor Co were disappointing.
Hyundai Motor posted a net profit of 28.16 billion won in the first-half, compared to 51.64 billion a year earlier.
"Hyundai Motor was quite disappointing," said Lee of ING Barings. "We have it recommended as a 'buy' at the moment, but we're wondering whether we have to downgrade it."
Ricks of BZW was more optimistic.
"I think the auto industry will stay sluggish but Hyundai's second-half earnings should be quite a bit higher," he said.

Korea Electric Power Corp, South Korea's electricity monopoly, saw its first-half profits plunge 67 percent to 110.5 billion won from 333.5 billion won, largely because of a depreciating local currency and higher oil prices.
Ricks said falling oil prices and a July 1 rate hike of 5.9 percent would combine to boost KEPCO's second-half profits.
"If oil prices remain low throughout the rest of the year, companies that import a lot of oil, like KEPCO, will benefit."
But POSCO, the world's second largest steel maker, saw its interim net profits soar 40.8 percent to 543.23 billion won.
"POSCO certainly is encouraging," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd. "They are going to have a record year this year."
(Conversion: $1 = 894.3 won)
